https://www.coventrytelegraph.net/news/c.text: Police have charged a man over the death of Keaton Slater in Coventry after he was extradited from Latvia. Dolars Aleksanders was detained last month and flown to the UK yesterday (August 5). Schoolboy Keaton, 12, was killed in an alleged hit-and-run on Radford Road in June 2024. Aleksanders, 23, was wanted on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving but allegedly fled to Latvia. West Midlands Police worked with the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), the National Crime Agency (NCA), and other partner organisations to bring Aleksanders back to the UK. He was flown into Gatwick Airport yesterday and was then taken into custody in the West Midlands. READ MORE: Smiling thug left man needing surgery after 'frenzied' bottle attack in Coventry READ MORE: Coventry dad who dedicated his life to helping young people dies aged just 36 Aleksanders has now been charged with causing death by dangerous driving. He has been remanded to appear before Birmingham Magistrates' Court today (August 6). A spokesman for West Midlands Police said: “ A man has been charged over the death of 12-year-old Keaton Slater in Coventry after he was extradited from Latvia. Dolars Aleksanders was detained last month, and we have since worked with other agencies, including the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and National Crime Agency (NCA), to bring him back to the UK. “ Aleksanders was flown into Gatwick Airport yesterday and was then transported to a custody block in the West Midlands. He has now been charged with causing death by dangerous driving following the fatal hit-and-run collision in Radford Road in June 2024. “ He has been remanded to appear before Birmingham Magistrates' Court today (August 6). His parents continue to be supported by specially trained officers, and they have been fully updated around these developments. We thank them for their patience and support during our investigation. ” Ben Samples, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “We have decided to charge Dolars Aleksanders with one count of causing death by dangerous driving following a police investigation into a fatal road traffic collision that led to the death of Keaton Slater. Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court to pursue criminal proceedings. “CPS West Midlands has worked closely with West Midlands Police , Home Office, the Latvian authorities, Europol, the Joint International Crime Centre (JICC), CPS International, and our Extradition Unit to bring Mr Aleksanders back to face proceedings in a UK court for an alleged crime that took place here.” Sign up for CoventryLive newsletters to stay up to date with the latest news across Coventry and Warwickshire . https://nineoclock.ro/chery-group-enters.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Chery Group entered the global Top 10 automakers in the first half of 2026, driven by strong international sales growth and the expansion of the new energy vehicle (NEV) segment. The performance further strengthens the global ecosystem of which iCAUR is part, Chery Group’s strategic NEV brand preparing to launch in Romania, the first European market signed for the brand’s development. In the first half of 2026, Chery Group reached a 4.1% share of global automotive sales, ranking ninth worldwide. During the same period, the Group sold 475,238 NEVs, an increase of 32.3% compared with the previous year. Growth was also supported by performance in Europe, where new energy vehicle sales reached 86,000 units, up 385% compared with the same period in 2025. International expansion continued in July, when Chery Group surpassed 200,000 vehicles exported in a single month for the first time. Globally, the Group serves more than 20.16 million users, including 5.56 million outside China, and operates in more than 130 countries and regions. The Group’s global development is supported by an extensive research and development infrastructure, with Chery operating eight R&D centres across Europe, Asia and North America. Within this ecosystem, iCAUR contributes to Chery Group’s global development strategy in the new energy vehicle segment, combining electrified technologies, distinctive design and an approach built around the Urban Outdoor Adventure concept. One of the models supporting the brand’s international development is the iCAUR V23. Launched in China at the end of 2024, the model has surpassed 100,000 units sold globally and is present in more than 20 countries and regions. The V23 received the Red Dot Design Award 2026 and achieved a five-star rating in the ASEAN NCAP safety assessment. The model also ranked first in the Midsize Battery Electric SUV segment in the J.D. Power 2026 China New Energy Vehicle Appeal Study. iCAUR V27, the next stage of the brand’s development in Europe For Europe, the next stage of iCAUR’s development will be supported by the V27, the brand’s global flagship and the first model planned for the Romanian market. Romania is iCAUR’s first signed European market, while AUTO ITALIA is the first confirmed partner group for the brand’s development in Europe. The official launch of iCAUR in Romania is scheduled for October 2026, with the V27 expected to become commercially available at the beginning of 2027. The first iCAUR V27 prototypes have already been shipped to Romania and are scheduled to arrive in September 2026. They will support the brand’s pre-launch promotion and preparations for local activities ahead of the official iCAUR launch on the Romanian market. The iCAUR V27 features the Golden REEV system, developed to combine an electric driving experience with the range required for long-distance travel. The system uses a 1.5T engine as a generator and achieves thermal efficiency of up to 44.5%. In the configuration intended for the V27, the system provides more than 150 km of electric range and a total combined range of more than 1,000 km. The model also features the i-AWD intelligent all-wheel-drive system, designed to automatically adapt to different driving conditions, as well as V2L functionality, which allows external electrical equipment to be powered directly from the vehicle. With the launch of iCAUR, AUTO ITALIA is continuing to expand Chery Group’s portfolio on the Romanian market, one year after the introduction of the CHERY brand in Romania. iCAUR will complement the Group’s portfolio with a proposition aimed at customers seeking extended range, versatility and a model suited both to everyday use and to travel and outdoor experiences. Further information regarding the launch of iCAUR in Romania, the commercial network and the portfolio intended for the local market will be announced in the coming period. https://www.dw.com/en/magyar-vs-moscow-h.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MPdA The close and friendly ties between Hungary and Russia ended when Peter Magyar became prime minister earlier this year Image: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP Advertisement While Viktor Orban was in power, no other EU member state was as pro-Russian as Hungary . Indeed, the former prime minister's apparent eagerness to be of service to the Russian president earned him the nickname "Putin's pinscher" or "Kremlin agent." For years, Hungary was seen as a security risk both in the EU and NATO . Russian spies were able to operate in the country largely unhindered for a long time. In February, it came to light that former Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto had passed on confidential information from EU meetings to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov . All this came to an end in May , when the new government headed by Peter Magyar took office . An unambiguous signal to Moscow In a clear departure from the government line under Orban, Hungary's new prime minister has already heavily criticized Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine several times. The government also recently declared Russia a threat to Hungary's national security. This week, it took its biggest step yet against Russia, expelling 10 Russian diplomats for engaging in activities "that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention," as announced by Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban (no relation to the former prime minister). Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban announced this week that Hungary was expelling 10 Russian embassy staff for activities 'that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention' Image: Daniel Vogl/dpa/picture alliance Although Orban did not provide any more details, the phrase is generally understood to mean that the diplomats in question were spies. The minister went on to say that the decision "protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," adding, "It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules." Back to old alliances The minister's brief announcement immediately generated a huge number of headlines and comments — hardly surprising given that this was not only evidence of the government's 180° turn on the country's policy toward Russia but also one of the toughest diplomatic sanctions targeting Moscow since the collapse of communism in 1989/1990. Speaking to Hungarian news website Index, secret service expert Peter Tarjani said that this was "not a diplomatic conflict, but a serious secret service matter" and that with this decision, Hungary was simultaneously returning "to the mainstream of its allies' security policy." Political scientist and leading Hungarian Russia expert Andras Racz told the Hungarian national news agency MTI that Hungary was the only EU and NATO member not to have made such an expulsion in recent years. Racz said that such a step "should really have been taken four-and-a-half years ago," adding that "Hungary is now settling its old debt with its allies." Reliance on Russian gas? Under Viktor Orban, Hungary was in fact the only EU country never to unreservedly condemn Russia's all-out war against Ukraine. Indeed, during the last two years of his rule, Orban even blamed Ukraine and the West for Russia's aggression. The Russian Embassy in Budapest Image: Aled Betts/cc-by/Wikimedia Commons But long before that — even after he came to power back in 2010 — Viktor Orban took a markedly pro-Russian line , which he justified, among other things, with the claim that Hungary was more dependent on Russian energy supplies than almost any other country in the region. His government's repeated assertion that Russian gas was cheaper has long been disproved. What's more, the expansion of the Paks nuclear power plant with Russian support will cost Hungary dearly for decades to come. In the light of all this, Orban's close ties to Russia remain a mystery. Absurd situations For Hungary, this closeness to Russia often led to absurd situations in which the country's national security was put at risk. At the same time, Orban repeatedly told his critics that it was they who were a threat to Hungary's sovereignty. For example, Russian secret service agents for years took part in military-style training exercises in the far-right scene right up until 2016. Starting in 2012, Russian secret service operatives for years stole huge amounts of data from the Hungarian Foreign Ministry and other Hungarian authorities without the government ever publicly condemning it. In 2019, Russia got permission to move the headquarters of the International Investment Bank (IIB) to Budapest. The IIB was known as the "spy bank" because its leadership was made up of individuals linked to or associated with Russia's FSB intelligence service. It was only after the US imposed sanctions on the bank in 2023 that it left Hungary again. Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi has warned multiple times in recent years that Hungary had become a "logistical center and deployment zone for Russian secret services," thereby putting the whole region at risk. Rejection of Orban's pro-Russian course Orban's strictly pro-Russian course was laterally rejected by many Hungarians. Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban (left, pictured here with Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2025) maintained close ties with Russia while he was in power Image: Alexander Nemenov/Pool/AFP The decidedly pro-European and pro-Western orientation of Peter Magyar and his Tisza party had a considerable role to play in their election victory earlier this year. The EU flag was often seen and spontaneous cries of "Russians, go home" often heard at election rallies last spring. Unlike Viktor Orban, Magyar and leading politicians in his Tisza party are convinced that Hungary's place is exclusively in Europe and that the country should only maintain pragmatic, low-level relations with Russia. Nevertheless, many observers and experts are surprised at how radically the Magyar government has turned away from Russia. Andras Telkes, the former deputy head of Hungary's foreign intelligence service (IH), wrote in the newspaper Nepszava that the expulsion of diplomats shows that the presence of Russian secret services in Hungary obviously runs "very deep" and that the country has a serious problem. Telkes says that the expulsion of 10 diplomats will help rebuild trust in Hungary in the eyes of the secret services of its NATO allies. At the same time, he emphasizes the scale of the move: "Expelling two or three people would have been a sign. Expelling 10 people already means war." Telkes went on to say that the move creates a serious security problem for Hungary. Will Moscow turn off the taps? The spokeswoman for the Russian Foreign Ministry condemned the expulsion of Russian diplomats in unusually strong terms: She spoke of a "Russophobe lobby in Budapest" and announced a "hard and painful" response. Russian lawmaker Andrey Kolesnik, a member of the State Duma's Defense Committee, said that halting gas supplies to Hungary would have to be considered. Hungary's Foreign Minister Anita Orban knows more about such Russian threats than anyone else in the new Hungarian government: She wrote her doctoral thesis in 2007 on Russia's energy policy in Central Europe. A year later, she published a book entitled "Power, Energy, and the New Russian Imperialism." This article was originally published in German. Composite: World Central Kitchen/PA View image in fullscreen John Chapman, Jim Henderson and James Kirby, three British workers who were killed in an air strike in Gaza. Composite: World Central Kitchen/PA Gaza Inquest into British aid workers killed in Gaza may call on Israeli and UK military chiefs Lawyer tells hearing that families wish to know whether weaponry involved in deaths was made in Britain Steven Morris Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Israeli and UK military commanders could be requested to give evidence to an inquest concerning three British workers killed in Gaza when aid vehicles they were travelling in were hit by an airstrike. It is also possible that the inquest into the deaths of John Chapman, 57, Jim Henderson, 33, and James Kirby, 47 , may examine whether the weaponry that killed the men was made in the UK. Until now, the focus of the inquest has been on the role played by the aid organisation in charge of the convoy and the security firm that was protecting it. But at a pre-inquest review, Maria Voisin, the senior coroner for Avon, indicated that the scope of the final hearing would probably be widened to include the role of Israeli authorities in the deaths. The coroner said she was “minded” to designate the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and the colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, as “interested parties” for the inquest. Interested parties are often relatives of the person who died or an organisation or individual believed to be closely involved in what happened. Israeli military authorities last month said they would not open criminal investigations into the strike which, along with the three Britons, also killed the Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom , and one each from Poland, Palestine and the US. The UK, Australian and Canadian governments called the Israeli decision “shameful”. View image in fullscreen One of the vehicles in which employees of the World Central Kitchen were killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza in 2024. Photograph: Reuters In a written submission to the court, Pete Weatherby KC, for Henderson, compared the case to that of the novichok attack by the Russian state in Salisbury, in which the British woman Dawn Sturgess was killed. In that case, the high court in London ruled the lack of any criminal investigation by the Russian authorities and the strong public concern surrounding the circumstances of Sturgess’ death necessitated the expansion of the scope of the investigation. Ed Sheeran says situation in Gaza ‘unjustifiable’ in first show since tour plunged into turmoil Read more Lawyers for the three men accepted that it was possible Israel would not cooperate with the inquest but called for UK ministers to try to apply pressure if needed. Another element the families are keen to have investigated is the role the British military may have played in the incident in April 2024. Weatherby’s submission says that a Royal Air Force surveillance plane spent about five hours above Gaza on the day of the attack, seemingly returning to base minutes before the airstrikes were launched. The families want to know what, if any, surveillance the plane gathered about the convoy – and what was shared with the Israeli authorities. The barrister also told the review hearing in Flax Bourton, near Bristol, it was a “matter of public concern” and “great importance to the family” to find out if the weaponry that killed the men was made in the UK. Voisin said she was open minded about which issues the inquest would consider and would keep some under review. “It’s very much a case of throwing the net wide at the moment,” she said. In a statement, Henderson’s father, Neil Henderson, said: “We hope the coroner will carry out a thorough investigation into the attack that killed Jim and the others [including] an exploration of all the issues relevant to his death, encompassing the decisions and policies leading to the attack, and what role, if any, UK authorities or military equipment originating from the UK may have played.” A further pre-inquest review will take place in March. No date for the final hearing has been set.
